constellations.name: Orion
constellations.description: One of the most recognizable constellations, depicting a hunter with a distinctive belt of three stars.
constellations.mythology: In Greek mythology, Orion was a giant huntsman placed among the stars by Zeus. Son of Poseidon, he was the most handsome of men, killed by a scorpion sent by Gaia. This is why Orion and Scorpius are never in the sky at the same time.

stars.name: Alnitak
stars.starType: Blue supergiant (illuminates the nearby Flame Nebula)

constellations.practicalUses: Because Orion's Belt sits almost exactly on the celestial equator, it rises due east and sets due west from nearly anywhere on Earth, making it a handy way to find true east and west and a widely used seasonal marker for the start of winter in the north.
constellations.culturalSignificance: Ancient Egyptians linked Orion's Belt to the god Osiris, while many Aboriginal Australian traditions see the same three stars as young men, a canoe, or other figures entirely different from a hunter.

constellations.name: Taurus
constellations.description: The Bull, marked by fiery orange Aldebaran and the sparkling Pleiades cluster nestled at its shoulder.
constellations.mythology: Taurus is Zeus in disguise, transformed into a magnificent white bull to approach Europa. He carried her across the sea to Crete, where she became queen, giving her name to the continent of Europe.

stars.name: Pleiades
stars.starType: Open star cluster of hot young blue stars (the 'Seven Sisters')

stars.name: Hyades
stars.starType: Open star cluster, one of the nearest to Earth

constellations.practicalUses: The dawn reappearance of the Pleiades each year was widely used by farming and seafaring cultures to time planting, harvest, and the start of the sailing season.
constellations.culturalSignificance: The Pleiades are called Matariki by the Māori, whose reappearance marks the Māori New Year, and Krittika in Hindu tradition; Japanese know the cluster as Subaru, and Aboriginal Australian traditions across the continent also track its rising as a seasonal calendar.

constellations.name: Auriga
constellations.description: The Charioteer, a pentagon of stars anchored by golden Capella, one of the sky's brightest stars.
constellations.mythology: Auriga is Erichthonius, the legendary king of Athens who invented the four-horse chariot. Capella represents the goat Amalthea that suckled the infant Zeus.

stars.name: Capella
stars.starType: Yellow giant star (actually a close pair of yellow giants)

stars.name: Mahasim
stars.starType: White star with a chemically peculiar, strongly magnetic surface

stars.name: Almaaz
stars.starType: Yellow-white supergiant, dimmed every 27 years by a huge dark companion disk

stars.name: Haedus I
stars.starType: Orange bright giant, an eclipsing binary nicknamed 'the Kid'

constellations.practicalUses: Capella's brightness and high northern position made it a dependable marker of the winter sky, and its early evening rising was noted as a sign of the changing season.
constellations.culturalSignificance: Chinese astronomers grouped Auriga's stars into Wǔchē, the 'Five Chariots,' associating them with five legendary emperors and with the harvest of China's staple grain crops.

constellations.name: Lepus
constellations.description: The Hare, a small, faint huddle of stars crouching quietly beneath Orion's feet.
constellations.mythology: Lepus is the hare hunted by Orion and his dogs. It was placed beneath Orion's feet to represent the eternal chase across the winter sky.

stars.name: Mu Leporis
stars.starType: Blue-white subgiant with a chemically peculiar spectrum

constellations.practicalUses: Too dim for navigation on its own, Lepus mainly served skywatchers as a marker of the sky region just south of Orion, useful for tracking the same winter season as its much brighter neighbor.
constellations.culturalSignificance: Lepus carries little documented mythology outside the Greek image of a hare fleeing Orion's hounds, though its position beneath the great hunter made it a recognizable fixture in many naked-eye sky traditions.

constellations.name: Canis Major
constellations.description: The Greater Dog, home to Sirius, the brightest star in the entire night sky.
constellations.mythology: Canis Major is one of Orion's hunting dogs. Sirius was sacred to ancient Egyptians as its heliacal rising marked the flooding of the Nile and the start of their new year.

stars.name: Sirius
stars.starType: White main-sequence star, the brightest star in the night sky, with a white dwarf companion (Sirius B)

stars.name: Aludra
stars.starType: Blue supergiant, one of the most luminous stars known

constellations.practicalUses: Sirius's first visible rise before dawn each year let ancient Egyptians predict the annual Nile flood, anchoring their calendar so precisely that it effectively defined their civil year.
constellations.culturalSignificance: Egyptians linked Sirius to the goddess Isis, Chinese astronomers called it the 'Celestial Wolf' (Tiānláng), and the Dogon people of Mali preserved an oral tradition about Sirius that anthropologists have studied for its unusual astronomical detail.

constellations.name: Canis Minor
constellations.description: The Little Dog, a compact pair of stars led by bright Procyon.
constellations.mythology: Canis Minor is Orion's second hunting dog. Procyon means 'before the dog' in Greek, as it rises just before Sirius. In Egyptian mythology both were associated with the flooding of the Nile.

stars.name: Procyon
stars.starType: Yellow-white subgiant star with a faint white dwarf companion

constellations.practicalUses: Procyon's name, meaning 'before the dog' in Greek, reflects its old practical role as an early warning that Sirius was about to rise.
constellations.culturalSignificance: Like Sirius, Procyon was tied by ancient Egyptians to the Nile's flood cycle, making it one of several 'dog stars' watched closely across the ancient Mediterranean world.

constellations.name: Gemini
constellations.description: The Twins, marked by the bright paired stars Castor and Pollux sitting side by side.
constellations.mythology: Castor and Pollux were twins, the Dioscuri. Pollux was immortal, son of Zeus, while Castor was mortal. When Castor died, Pollux asked Zeus to share his immortality. Zeus placed them together in the stars, where they remain inseparable.

stars.name: Castor
stars.starType: White main-sequence star (actually a system of six stars)

stars.name: Pollux
stars.starType: Orange giant star, known to host a giant planet

stars.name: Mekbuda
stars.starType: Yellow supergiant, a pulsating variable star

constellations.practicalUses: The close pairing of Castor and Pollux made them easy reference points for tracking the ecliptic, and their rising was historically used to mark the approach of summer in the northern hemisphere.
constellations.culturalSignificance: Babylonian astronomers saw these stars as the 'Great Twins,' the gods Meslamtaea and Lugalirra, a tradition older than the Greek Castor and Pollux story; Chinese astronomy places the same region within the Jing (Well) lunar mansion.

constellations.name: Monoceros
constellations.description: The Unicorn, a faint, sprawling constellation tucked inside the Winter Triangle.
constellations.mythology: Monoceros was introduced by Dutch cartographer Petrus Plancius in 1612, possibly inspired by the unicorn mentioned in the Old Testament. The unicorn was a symbol of purity in medieval European tradition.
constellations.practicalUses: Too dim to be useful for navigation or timekeeping, Monoceros mainly serves modern stargazers as rich hunting ground for star clusters and nebulae hidden between brighter, more famous constellations.
constellations.culturalSignificance: Monoceros was invented by Dutch cartographer Petrus Plancius in the early 1600s, so it carries no ancient mythology; its unicorn imagery drew on medieval European legend rather than any older cultural tradition.

constellations.name: Cancer
constellations.description: The Crab, the dimmest constellation of the zodiac, best known for the Beehive star cluster at its center.
constellations.mythology: Hera sent Cancer the Crab to distract Heracles during his battle with the Hydra. The crab pinched his foot but was quickly crushed. As reward for its loyalty, Hera placed it among the stars.

stars.name: Beehive Cluster
stars.starType: Open star cluster (Praesepe/M44) with roughly 1,000 member stars

constellations.practicalUses: Cancer once marked the point where the Sun reached its highest point in the sky at the summer solstice, which is why that latitude is still called the Tropic of Cancer today.
constellations.culturalSignificance: Ancient Egyptian sky charts, including the Dendera zodiac, depicted this constellation as a scarab beetle, a sacred symbol of rebirth, rather than as a crab.

constellations.name: Hydra
constellations.description: The Water Snake, the longest and largest of all 88 constellations, slithering across a quarter of the sky.
constellations.mythology: Hydra is the many-headed water serpent slain by Heracles as his second labor. For every head cut off, two grew back. Heracles solved this by cauterizing each stump with fire.
constellations.practicalUses: Hydra's great length made it a useful backdrop for tracking the slow progression of the seasons, since different parts of the snake cross the night sky throughout the year.
constellations.culturalSignificance: Chinese astronomers divided Hydra's long body among several lunar mansions, including Willow (Liǔ) and Star (Xīng), each carrying its own symbolic meaning rather than being read as a single serpent.

constellations.name: Leo
constellations.description: The Lion, marked by bright Regulus and a curved row of stars forming its mane, called the Sickle.
constellations.mythology: Leo represents the Nemean Lion, killed by Heracles as his first labor. The lion's hide was impervious to weapons, so Heracles strangled it with bare hands and used its own claws to skin it. Zeus honored its strength by placing it in the stars.
constellations.practicalUses: Leo's appearance high in spring skies made it a seasonal marker for planting time in several farming cultures of the Mediterranean and Near East.
constellations.culturalSignificance: Babylonian astronomers already recognized this pattern as a great lion, UR.GU.LA, centuries before the Greeks, and Egyptian tradition linked the lion to the sun's strength during the hot season when the Nile began to flood.

constellations.name: Ursa Major
constellations.description: The Great Bear, home to the Big Dipper, one of the most familiar star patterns in the sky.
constellations.mythology: Zeus fell in love with the nymph Callisto and Hera transformed her into a bear in jealousy. When her son Arcas nearly killed her while hunting, Zeus placed them both in the stars. Hera convinced Poseidon never to let them sink below the horizon, which is why they are circumpolar.

stars.name: Megrez
stars.starType: White main-sequence star, the faintest of the Big Dipper's stars

stars.name: Alioth
stars.starType: White star with a peculiar, strongly magnetic surface

stars.name: Mizar
stars.starType: White main-sequence star, forms a famous naked-eye double with Alcor

constellations.practicalUses: The two 'pointer stars' at the front of the Dipper's bowl line up almost exactly with Polaris, making this constellation the most common way for northern-hemisphere skywatchers to find true north.
constellations.culturalSignificance: Chinese astronomers called it Běidǒu, the Northern Dipper, using its handle's rotation through the seasons as a natural calendar; many Native American traditions saw the bowl as a bear pursued by hunters represented in the handle stars, while Hindu tradition names its seven stars the Saptarshi, the Seven Sages.

constellations.name: Corvus
constellations.description: The Crow, a small, neat quadrilateral of stars perched beside Virgo.
constellations.mythology: Apollo sent a crow to fetch water. The crow was distracted by a fig tree and returned late with a water snake as excuse. Apollo placed all three in the sky, the crow forever unable to drink from the nearby cup.

stars.name: Algorab
stars.starType: White main-sequence star (same star as Delta Corvi)

constellations.practicalUses: Its compact, easily traced shape made Corvus a useful minor waypoint for skywatchers navigating the region between the much larger constellations Virgo and Hydra.
constellations.culturalSignificance: Chinese astronomers folded Corvus into Zhěn, the Chariot, one of the 28 lunar mansions used to track the Moon's monthly path across the sky.

constellations.name: Virgo
constellations.description: The Maiden, the largest constellation of the zodiac, holding an ear of wheat marked by the star Spica.
constellations.mythology: Virgo is Demeter, goddess of the harvest, or her daughter Persephone. When Persephone descends to the underworld each autumn, Demeter's grief causes winter. Spica, held in the maiden's hand, represents a sheaf of wheat.
constellations.practicalUses: Virgo's appearance was tied to harvest time in many farming societies, and the wheat-sheaf imagery around Spica made it a natural seasonal marker for the grain harvest.
constellations.culturalSignificance: Babylonian astronomers pictured this region as 'the Furrow,' associated with the grain goddess Shala, a farming symbolism that closely parallels the Greek image of a harvest maiden; Chinese astronomy splits the same stars among several lunar mansions.

constellations.name: Centaurus
constellations.description: The Centaur, a large southern constellation containing Alpha Centauri, our closest neighboring star system.
constellations.mythology: Centaurus is Chiron, the wisest of the centaurs and tutor to Achilles. Accidentally wounded by Heracles's poisoned arrow, he suffered eternally as an immortal until Zeus granted him release among the stars.

stars.name: Alpha Centauri
stars.starType: Yellow main-sequence star (Sun-like), part of the nearest star system to the Sun

constellations.practicalUses: Alpha and Beta Centauri, known as 'the Pointers,' have long been used by southern-hemisphere navigators to locate the Southern Cross and, from it, the south celestial pole.
constellations.culturalSignificance: Many Aboriginal Australian traditions weave the Pointer stars into a larger sky-story involving the nearby dark 'Emu in the Sky,' reading the dark dust lanes of the Milky Way alongside the bright stars.

constellations.name: Crux
constellations.description: The Southern Cross, the smallest constellation in the sky but one of the most instantly recognizable.
constellations.mythology: Crux was known to ancient Greeks but sank below the European horizon over millennia. Portuguese explorers rediscovered it in the 15th century and saw it as a divine cross guiding their voyages into the southern seas.
constellations.practicalUses: Crux's long axis points almost directly toward the south celestial pole, making it the primary tool navigators and travelers in the southern hemisphere have used for centuries to find true south.
constellations.culturalSignificance: It appears on the national flags of Australia, New Zealand, Brazil, and other southern nations; Aboriginal Australian traditions incorporate it into the 'Emu in the Sky' dark constellation, and Māori tradition knows it as Te Punga, the anchor of a great canoe.

constellations.name: Boötes
constellations.description: The Herdsman, a kite-shaped constellation led by Arcturus, the brightest star of the northern sky.
constellations.mythology: Boötes is Arcas driving the Great Bear around the pole, or Icarius, an Athenian farmer taught winemaking by Dionysus. When shepherds who drank his wine thought they were poisoned and killed him, Dionysus placed him among the stars.
constellations.practicalUses: Arcturus's brightness and position made it a reliable marker for the arrival of spring, and the saying 'follow the arc to Arcturus' has long helped skywatchers star-hop from the Big Dipper's handle.
constellations.culturalSignificance: Arabic astronomers named Arcturus 'Al Simak al-Rāmiḥ,' the lofty lance-bearer, one of two prominent stars they called 'the raised ones' (the other being Spica in Virgo), a naming tradition that fed directly into medieval European star catalogs.

constellations.name: Libra
constellations.description: The Scales, the only zodiac constellation to represent an object rather than a person or animal.
constellations.mythology: Libra represents the scales of justice held by Astraea, goddess of justice associated with Virgo. The star names Zubenelgenubi and Zubeneschamali are Arabic for 'southern claw' and 'northern claw', remnants of when they belonged to Scorpius.

stars.name: Zubenelakrab
stars.starType: Orange giant star (historically confused with a neighboring star of nearly the same name)

stars.name: Zubenelhakrabi
stars.starType: Orange giant star, known to host two planets

constellations.practicalUses: When the Sun passed through this part of the sky in antiquity, day and night were of equal length, and the scales came to symbolize that seasonal balance at the autumnal equinox.
constellations.culturalSignificance: Babylonian astronomers already called this pattern the 'Scales' (zibānītu) roughly 2,000 years before the Greeks adopted the same image, associating it with the sun god Shamash as patron of truth and justice.

constellations.name: Corona Borealis
constellations.description: The Northern Crown, a small, graceful semicircle of stars anchored by bright Alphecca.
constellations.mythology: Corona Borealis is the crown of Ariadne, who helped Theseus slay the Minotaur. Abandoned by Theseus, she was found by Dionysus who made her his wife. At their wedding he gave her a golden crown, which Zeus placed among the stars.

stars.name: Beta CrB
stars.starType: Yellow-white star with a peculiar magnetic spectrum

constellations.practicalUses: Too faint and small for practical navigation, Corona Borealis mainly served skywatchers as a memorable landmark for orienting themselves between the larger constellations Boötes and Hercules nearby.
constellations.culturalSignificance: The Shawnee told of it as the 'Celestial Sisters,' star maidens who descended in a basket to dance in a circle on Earth, while Chinese astronomers saw the same stars as Guànsuǒ, a coiled rope representing a prison.

constellations.name: Ursa Minor
constellations.description: The Little Bear, home to Polaris, the star that currently marks true north.
constellations.mythology: Ursa Minor is Arcas, the son of Callisto, placed in the sky by Zeus alongside his mother. Polaris at the tip of its tail has guided navigators for millennia. Ancient Greeks called it Cynosura, the guiding star.

stars.name: Polaris
stars.starType: Yellow-white supergiant, today's North Star (a pulsating Cepheid variable)

stars.name: Kochab
stars.starType: Orange giant star, an ancient pole star

constellations.practicalUses: Because Polaris sits almost directly above Earth's rotational axis, it barely moves in the sky, making it the most important star in the northern hemisphere for judging latitude and finding direction.
constellations.culturalSignificance: Chinese astronomy placed the celestial pole near the seat of the emperor in the Ziwei enclosure, and Polynesian navigators knew Polaris as Hōkūpaʻa, the 'fixed star,' using its height above the horizon to judge how far north or south they had sailed.

constellations.name: Hercules
constellations.description: The Kneeler, a large but faint constellation home to the Hercules Cluster, one of the finest star clusters visible from the north.
constellations.mythology: Heracles was the greatest Greek hero, son of Zeus. Hera drove him mad and he killed his family. As penance the Oracle assigned him twelve labors. He completed them all, earning immortality and a place among the stars.

stars.name: Alpha Herculis
stars.starType: Red giant star (a huge pulsating variable, one of the largest stars visible to the naked eye)

constellations.practicalUses: Hercules is too faint to have served as a major navigational marker, but its position between brighter neighbors made it a useful reference point for locating the globular cluster M13 with a telescope.
constellations.culturalSignificance: The kneeling-figure pattern predates the Greek hero legend attached to it; an earlier Babylonian tradition associated the same stars with a kneeling or struggling figure before it was identified with Heracles.

constellations.name: Ophiuchus
constellations.description: The Serpent Bearer, a large constellation straddling the zodiac and wrestling the neighboring constellation Serpens.
constellations.mythology: Ophiuchus is Asclepius, god of medicine, so skilled he could resurrect the dead. Hades was alarmed and Zeus struck him down. Apollo convinced Zeus to honor him among the stars. His image with a serpent became the basis for the caduceus, symbol of medicine.

stars.name: Zeta Ophiuchi
stars.starType: Blue main-sequence star, a massive runaway star

constellations.practicalUses: Because the Sun actually passes through Ophiuchus every year, astronomers tracking the ecliptic closely have long had to account for it even though it was never counted among the traditional twelve zodiac signs.
constellations.culturalSignificance: Some historians believe Babylonian astronomers recognized an earlier serpent-holding figure in this region, linked to the god Nirah, though the connection is unconfirmed; the Greeks later mapped the same stars onto the serpent-holding healer Asclepius.

constellations.name: Scorpius
constellations.description: The Scorpion, one of the most vivid constellations in the sky, with the fiery red star Antares glowing at its heart.
constellations.mythology: Scorpius is the scorpion sent by Gaia to kill Orion. Zeus placed both in the sky on opposite sides, so when Scorpius rises in the east, Orion flees below the western horizon. Antares means 'rival of Mars' and glows with a deep reddish hue.

stars.name: Antares
stars.starType: Red supergiant, one of the largest known stars

stars.name: Shaula
stars.starType: Blue subgiant star with a hidden neutron-star companion

constellations.practicalUses: Scorpius's curling tail rises low in southern skies during summer evenings, and its appearance has long served as a seasonal marker heralding the warm months in the northern hemisphere.
constellations.culturalSignificance: Hawaiian navigators saw the same curved shape as Maui's fishhook, Ka Makau Nui o Maui, used in legend to pull the islands up from the sea, while Chinese astronomy places these same stars in the tail of the Azure Dragon of the East.

constellations.name: Lyra
constellations.description: The Lyre, a small but brilliant constellation marked by blue-white Vega, one of the brightest stars in the sky.
constellations.mythology: Lyra is the lyre of Orpheus, the greatest musician in Greek mythology. His music moved even Hades to allow his dead wife Eurydice to return. After his death, Zeus placed his lyre in the sky still singing.

stars.name: Vega
stars.starType: White main-sequence star, one of the most closely studied stars after the Sun

stars.name: Sheliak
stars.starType: White main-sequence star (eclipsing binary, the prototype of its class)

stars.name: Delta Lyrae
stars.starType: Red giant star (part of a wide double star)

stars.name: Zeta Lyrae
stars.starType: White main-sequence star (chemically peculiar, close double)

stars.name: Epsilon Lyrae
stars.starType: Yellow-white main-sequence star, part of the famous 'Double Double'

constellations.practicalUses: Vega's brightness and steady position made it a key reference star for ancient astronomers, and because of Earth's slow axial wobble it will become the north pole star again in roughly 12,000 years.
constellations.culturalSignificance: In Chinese tradition Vega is Zhīnǚ, the Weaver Girl, separated from her lover Niúláng (the star Altair) by the Milky Way and reunited only once a year, a legend still celebrated today at the Qixi Festival.

constellations.name: Sagittarius
constellations.description: The Archer, a centaur aiming his bow toward the dense heart of the Milky Way.
constellations.mythology: Sagittarius is a centaur drawing a bow aimed at Scorpius. His arrow points directly at Antares, the heart of the scorpion. The direction he aims also points toward the galactic center, the densest region of the Milky Way.
constellations.practicalUses: Because Sagittarius points toward the galactic center, it has long guided skywatchers to the richest, brightest part of the Milky Way, and its position along the zodiac marked the winter solstice in antiquity.
constellations.culturalSignificance: Babylonian astronomers already pictured this region as Pabilsag, a warrior god often shown carrying a bow, centuries before the Greek centaur-archer image took shape.

constellations.name: Aquila
constellations.description: The Eagle, a compact constellation marked by bright Altair, one corner of the Summer Triangle.
constellations.mythology: Aquila is the eagle of Zeus, who carried his thunderbolts. It also carried the young Ganymede to Olympus to become cupbearer to the gods. The eagle's position straddling the Milky Way represents its eternal flight.

stars.name: Altair
stars.starType: White main-sequence star, one of the fastest-spinning bright stars known

stars.name: Eta Aquilae
stars.starType: Yellow-white supergiant, a pulsating Cepheid variable

constellations.practicalUses: Altair's brightness and position near the celestial equator made it a dependable marker for late-summer nights across cultures in both hemispheres.
constellations.culturalSignificance: In Chinese and Japanese tradition Altair is the cowherd star, Niúláng or Hikoboshi, separated from his weaver-girl love across the Milky Way and reunited once a year, the same star-crossed legend celebrated in China's Qixi and Japan's Tanabata festivals.

constellations.name: Cygnus
constellations.description: The Swan, flying down the Milky Way with its wings outstretched, also known as the Northern Cross.
constellations.mythology: Cygnus is Zeus in swan form, who seduced Leda, producing Castor and Pollux and Helen of Troy. Others identify it with Orpheus transformed into a swan after death, placed near his lyre in the sky.

stars.name: Deneb
stars.starType: Blue-white supergiant, one of the most luminous stars known

stars.name: Albireo
stars.starType: Orange bright giant star, forms a famous colorful double with a blue companion

stars.name: Epsilon Cygni
stars.starType: Orange giant star (same star as Gienah)

constellations.practicalUses: Cygnus's position deep in the summer Milky Way made it a natural guide to the galaxy's bright star clouds, and its lead star Deneb serves as another anchor of the Summer Triangle.
constellations.culturalSignificance: Arabic astronomers named several of its stars, including Deneb (from 'dhanab,' meaning tail), preserving and transmitting older star knowledge that still shapes the constellation's names today.

constellations.name: Delphinus
constellations.description: The Dolphin, a small, charming diamond of stars sometimes called Job's Coffin.
constellations.mythology: Delphinus is the dolphin that persuaded Amphitrite to marry Poseidon, who rewarded it with a place in the stars. In another version it rescued the poet Arion from drowning sailors, carrying him safely to shore on its back.

stars.name: Gamma Delphini
stars.starType: White and orange double star, a popular small-telescope target

constellations.practicalUses: Too small and faint for major navigational use, Delphinus mostly served as a delightful landmark for skywatchers scanning the rich star fields of the summer Milky Way.
constellations.culturalSignificance: Its two brightest stars carry the unusual names Sualocin and Rotanev, a 19th-century astronomer's joke spelling 'Nicolaus Venator' backwards, a reminder that even recent human whimsy has left its mark on ancient star patterns.

constellations.name: Capricornus
constellations.description: The Sea Goat, an ancient zodiac constellation with the head of a goat and the tail of a fish.
constellations.mythology: Capricornus is Pan, who transformed into a goat-fish to escape the monster Typhon by leaping into the Nile. Zeus commemorated the clever escape by placing Pan in the sky.
constellations.practicalUses: In antiquity Capricornus marked the winter solstice, the point where the Sun reached its lowest point in the sky, which is why that latitude is still called the Tropic of Capricorn today.
constellations.culturalSignificance: The goat-fish image is far older than Greek mythology; Babylonian astronomers already depicted this same hybrid creature, called Suḫurmašu, as a symbol of the god Ea, more than 3,000 years ago.

constellations.name: Pegasus
constellations.description: The Winged Horse, best known for the Great Square, four stars that mark its body.
constellations.mythology: Pegasus sprang from Medusa's neck when Perseus beheaded her, fathered by Poseidon. Tamed by Bellerophon, they slew the Chimaera together. When Bellerophon tried to ride Pegasus to Olympus, Zeus sent a gadfly that threw him off, but placed the horse in the stars.

stars.name: Scheat
stars.starType: Red giant star, an irregular variable

stars.name: Sirrah
stars.starType: Blue-white main-sequence star, shared between Pegasus and Andromeda

constellations.practicalUses: The Great Square's large, easily traced shape made it a dependable seasonal marker for the arrival of autumn in the northern hemisphere.
constellations.culturalSignificance: One corner star of the Great Square, Sirrah, is shared with the neighboring constellation Andromeda, a reminder that constellation boundaries are a human bookkeeping convention rather than a fixed feature of the stars themselves.

constellations.name: Aquarius
constellations.description: The Water Bearer, one of the oldest constellations, shown pouring water from a jar.
constellations.mythology: Aquarius is Ganymede, the beautiful Trojan youth Zeus abducted as an eagle to serve as cupbearer to the gods. Some identify the figure with Deucalion, who survived the great flood, the water he pours representing the deluge.
constellations.practicalUses: Aquarius marks the point in the zodiac the Sun will occupy at the March equinox in coming centuries as Earth's axis slowly precesses, the origin of the popular idea of a coming 'Age of Aquarius.'
constellations.culturalSignificance: Ancient Egyptians linked this constellation to Hapi, the god of the Nile's annual flood, pouring the life-giving waters that fertilized the land each year.

constellations.name: Piscis Austrinus
constellations.description: The Southern Fish, home to bright Fomalhaut, sometimes called the 'Loneliest Star' for its isolated spot in a dim patch of sky.
constellations.mythology: Piscis Austrinus is the large fish that drinks the water poured by Aquarius. Fomalhaut was one of the four Royal Stars of ancient Persia, serving as guardian of the southern sky.

stars.name: Fomalhaut
stars.starType: White main-sequence star, surrounded by a debris disk with an orbiting planet

constellations.practicalUses: Fomalhaut's isolation and brightness made it easy to identify even under poor sky conditions, and ancient Persian astronomers counted it among the sky's four 'Royal Stars,' used as one of the guardian markers of the sky.
constellations.culturalSignificance: As one of the four Persian Royal Stars, Fomalhaut was believed to watch over the southern sky, a role paired with three other bright stars said to guard the north, east, and west.

constellations.name: Pisces
constellations.description: The Fish, a large, faint zodiac constellation showing two fish tied together by a cord.
constellations.mythology: Pisces is Aphrodite and Eros transformed into fish to escape the monster Typhon, tied together by a cord. The cord is represented by the star Al Rischa. They swim in opposite directions, reflecting the tension of their escape.

stars.name: Al Rischa
stars.starType: White star (close binary marking the traditional knot of the two fish's cords)

stars.name: Fumalsamakah
stars.starType: Blue-white star with a gaseous disk (a Be star)

constellations.practicalUses: Pisces currently contains the point where the Sun crosses the celestial equator each spring, making it the technical home of the vernal equinox used in calendar calculations.
constellations.culturalSignificance: Babylonian astronomers already depicted two connected fish in roughly this part of the sky, a symbol later folded into the Greek myth of Aphrodite and Eros fleeing the monster Typhon.

constellations.name: Andromeda
constellations.description: The Princess, home to the Andromeda Galaxy, the most distant object visible to the naked eye.
constellations.mythology: Andromeda was chained to a rock as sacrifice to the sea monster Cetus to appease Poseidon, angered by her mother Cassiopeia's vanity. Perseus rescued her using Medusa's severed head to turn the monster to stone. They married and were placed in the stars together.

stars.name: Sirrah
stars.starType: Blue-white main-sequence star, shared between Andromeda and Pegasus

stars.name: Almach
stars.starType: Orange bright giant star with a striking blue companion

stars.name: Upsilon Andromedae
stars.starType: Yellow-white main-sequence star, host to a multi-planet system

constellations.practicalUses: Andromeda's stars form a recognizable chain extending from the Great Square of Pegasus, helping skywatchers star-hop toward the faint smudge of the Andromeda Galaxy on dark nights.
constellations.culturalSignificance: Chinese astronomers folded these stars into Kuí, the 'Legs' mansion, whose much older Neolithic name was Tiānshǐ, the 'Celestial Pig' — an asterism linked to wisdom and scholarship, entirely unrelated to the Greek myth of the chained princess.

constellations.name: Cassiopeia
constellations.description: The Queen, a distinctive W-shaped constellation that never sets for observers in the far north.
constellations.mythology: Cassiopeia was the vain queen of Ethiopia who boasted she was more beautiful than the sea nymphs. Poseidon, furious, sent the sea monster Cetus to ravage the coast, and Andromeda had to be sacrificed until Perseus rescued her.

stars.name: Gamma Cassiopeiae
stars.starType: Blue subgiant star, an unpredictable eruptive variable

constellations.practicalUses: Being circumpolar and easy to recognize, Cassiopeia's W (or M, depending on the season) shape has long served as a reliable direction-finder, sitting roughly opposite the Big Dipper across Polaris.
constellations.culturalSignificance: Chinese astronomers grouped several of these stars into Wángliáng, named for a legendary charioteer, a very different figure from the vain queen of Greek myth.

constellations.name: Perseus
constellations.description: The Hero, home to the eclipsing variable star Algol and the dazzling Double Cluster.
constellations.mythology: Perseus was the son of Zeus, tasked with slaying Medusa whose gaze turned men to stone. Armed with a mirrored shield, he beheaded her, then used her head to turn the sea monster Cetus to stone and rescue Andromeda.

stars.name: Algol
stars.starType: Blue-white main-sequence star, the famous 'Demon Star' eclipsing binary

stars.name: Gorgonea Tertia
stars.starType: Red giant star (same star as Rho Persei, a semi-regular variable)

stars.name: Rho Persei
stars.starType: Red giant star (same star as Gorgonea Tertia, a semi-regular variable)

constellations.practicalUses: Algol's regular dimming every three days made it a natural subject for tracking and timekeeping once early astronomers noticed the pattern, long before the physical cause — an eclipsing binary star — was understood.
constellations.culturalSignificance: Arabic astronomers named the star Algol 'Ra's al-Ghūl,' the demon's head, likely reacting to its eerie, unexplained dimming, while Chinese astronomers placed it within Dàlíng, the Mausoleum asterism — two traditions independently marking the star as ominous.

constellations.name: Aries
constellations.description: The Ram, historically important as the vernal equinox point lay here roughly 2,000 years ago.
constellations.mythology: Aries is the ram with the golden fleece sent by Hermes to rescue Phrixus and Helle. Only Phrixus survived; he sacrificed the ram and hung its golden fleece in a sacred grove, the prize later sought by Jason and the Argonauts.
constellations.practicalUses: Because the Sun's position at the March equinox once fell within Aries, the constellation gave its name to the 'First Point of Aries,' a reference still used in astronomy and navigation even though precession has since shifted that point into Pisces.
constellations.culturalSignificance: The ram held deep religious significance in ancient Egypt, associated with the god Amun, while Babylonian astronomers recognized an earlier version of this constellation as a hired farmhand, MULLÚ.ḪUN.GÁ, before the ram imagery took hold.

constellations.name: Eridanus
constellations.description: The River, a long, winding constellation flowing from near Orion down to bright Achernar in the far south.
constellations.mythology: Eridanus is the celestial river into which Phaethon fell after losing control of the Sun chariot. Zeus struck Phaethon with a thunderbolt to stop the Earth from burning, and he fell blazing into the river.

stars.name: Achernar
stars.starType: Blue main-sequence star, one of the flattest (fastest-spinning) stars known

stars.name: Epsilon Eridani
stars.starType: Orange main-sequence star (Sun-like), one of the nearest stars known to host planets

stars.name: Ran
stars.starType: Orange main-sequence star (same star as Epsilon Eridani)

constellations.practicalUses: Eridanus's great length made it a marker of how far south the sky extended, since Achernar at its southern end was only visible to observers who traveled far enough south to see it clear the horizon.
constellations.culturalSignificance: Achernar's name comes from the Arabic 'ākhir an-nahr,' meaning 'end of the river,' reflecting how Arabic astronomers preserved and extended the Greek conception of a celestial river.
